title: Go SDK: standardize timeouts (transport defaults + per-request overrides) and consistent error wrapping
author: Mateusz Zielinski
release_notes: - Go SDK now applies consistent default HTTP transport timeouts and exposes per-request timeout overrides. Timeout and context-cancellation errors are wrapped consistently and can be inspected via errors.Is/errors.As.
description:
Context
Customers have reported inconsistent behavior between request timeouts vs context cancellation in the Go SDK (see SUP-9342). As part of the cross-SDK parity effort, we want explicit, predictable timeout defaults for non-streaming requests and safe behavior for streaming requests (avoid using http.Client.Timeout, which would terminate streams).

What this PR does
- Sets Go HTTP transport defaults in a single place (NewClient) so behavior is consistent across call sites.
- Adds per-request timeout overrides via request options (without forcing global client changes).
- Normalizes timeout/cancel error wrapping so callers can reliably detect: timeout vs user cancel vs other transport errors.

Details
1) Transport defaults (client-wide)
- Dial timeout: 10s
- KeepAlive: 30s
- TLSHandshakeTimeout: 10s
- ResponseHeaderTimeout: 30s (non-streaming calls)
- ExpectContinueTimeout: 1s
- IdleConnTimeout: 90s
- MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 20
Rationale: align with the SDK Behavior Standard (timeouts) while being conservative enough to avoid hung sockets/proxy stalls. Note: ResponseHeaderTimeout is applied at the transport level; for streaming calls we set it to 0 (disabled) and rely on per-request first-byte timeout.

2) Non-streaming request timeout (per-request)
- Default overall request timeout: 60s (implemented via context.WithTimeout around the request)
- Overridable per request: WithTimeout(d)
- Also supports WithResponseHeaderTimeout(d) for advanced tuning (rare).

3) Streaming requests
- Does NOT use http.Client.Timeout.
- Introduces stream-level first-byte timeout (default 30s) implemented via context deadline until the first SSE/event bytes are received.
- After first byte, no overall timeout is enforced; caller controls lifetime via context cancellation.
- Adds optional WithStreamIdleTimeout(d) (default disabled) for clients that want to fail on long stalls mid-stream (implemented in the stream reader loop; does not affect non-streaming).

4) Error wrapping / taxonomy
- New exported error wrappers in package redwood:
  - TimeoutError (wraps underlying error; includes Operation + Timeout)
  - ContextCanceledError (wraps context.Canceled)
  - ContextDeadlineExceededError (wraps context.DeadlineExceeded)
  - TransportError (wraps other net/http layer errors)
- Mapping rules:
  - errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) => ContextCanceledError
  - errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) OR net.Error.Timeout() => TimeoutError (or ContextDeadlineExceededError if the underlying is explicitly DeadlineExceeded)
  - everything else in the transport path => TransportError
Goal: users can reliably do errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) or errors.As(err, *redwood.TimeoutError) and get consistent results.

Tests
- Table-driven tests using httptest.Server to force:
  - delayed headers (ResponseHeaderTimeout)
  - delayed body after headers (overall WithTimeout)
  - context cancellation propagation
  - streaming: first-byte timeout vs cancel
- Adds regression tests for error inspection using errors.Is/errors.As.

Docs
- Updates Go SDK README (timeouts section) and inline godoc for ClientOptions + RequestOptions.

Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- Conformance harness scenarios for timeouts will be wired in ENG-2485.
- Streaming disconnect retry policy is handled in PR #200 / ADR-0138 workstream.

Checklist
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Docs/godoc updates
- [x] Changelog entry
- [x] Verified no use of http.Client.Timeout for streaming endpoints
commits: go: centralize default transport construction (timeouts + pooling)
go: add request options for WithTimeout / WithResponseHeaderTimeout / WithStreamFirstByteTimeout / WithStreamIdleTimeout
go: normalize timeout/cancel error wrapping and expose exported error types
tests: add httptest-based timeout and cancellation coverage
docs: document defaults and examples for per-request overrides
changed_areas: errors/map.go (mapping helper used across request/stream paths)
conversation:
Ibrahim Khan (review): Can we avoid introducing a new error type that hides context.DeadlineExceeded? A lot of users already key off errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded).
Mateusz Zielinski (author): Yep—updated mapping so the wrapper preserves errors.Is. TimeoutError now implements Unwrap() and we wrap context.DeadlineExceeded directly when it is the root cause. Added tests asserting errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) stays true.

Rafael Mendes (review): Default 60s overall for non-streaming is fine, but make sure retries (PR #198) don’t fight timeouts (e.g., attempt budget exceeds timeout).
Mateusz Zielinski (author): Good catch. The request context deadline is shared across attempts (retry loop uses the same ctx). Added a test where server delays force one retry and we ensure we still respect the original deadline.

Tomáš Novák (review): ResponseHeaderTimeout=30s might be too aggressive for some enterprise proxies. Any way to override globally?
Mateusz Zielinski (author): Added ClientOption WithDefaultResponseHeaderTimeout(d) and documented it. Also kept per-request override for edge cases.

Ethan Park (review): For streaming: first-byte timeout should match gateway expectations. We usually send first SSE event quickly, but some customers buffer until auth completes. 30s seems OK; document that proxies may buffer.
Mateusz Zielinski (author): Added note in README and a troubleshooting snippet. Also left WithStreamFirstByteTimeout(d) override.

CI note: Initial run failed due to a flaky timing assertion in streaming first-byte test (1/20). Adjusted to use a deterministic server channel signal and reran; green.

Final: Approvals from Ibrahim + Rafael + Tomáš. Squash merged.
closing_summary: Merged to main. This aligns Go SDK timeout behavior with the parity spec direction and resolves SUP-9342 by making timeout vs cancel behavior inspectable and consistent. Next PRs (streaming robustness + conformance harness) will build on these primitives.
